title: Event-Driven Architecture and Message Queues
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Event-Driven Architecture and Message Queues ##### Black Friday, 11:03 a.m. An e-commerce platform's order pipeline was a chain of synchronous HTTP calls: checkout service → inventory service → invoicing → email → warehouse. Under normal load, 900 ms end to end. Fine. At 11:03 on their biggest sale day, the invoicing service's database hit a connection limit. Response times went from 80 ms to 14 seconds. The inventory service, waiting synchronously, exhausted its own thread pool. Checkout began timing out. Customers retried, doubling the load. Within four minutes the entire order path was down — because one non-critical service in the middle of a chain got slow. The architecture that survives this is **event-driven**: checkout writes an event and returns; everything else consumes it at its own pace. Invoicing being slow means invoices are late, not that orders stop. A message broker sits between components and absorbs exactly this kind of shock. ##### Events, producers, consumers, brokers Four roles, and precise vocabulary helps. An **event** is an immutable statement of fact: *`order.paid` happened, here are the details, at this time*. Past tense, no instruction. This distinguishes it from a **command** (`ChargeCard` — do this thing), and the difference is architectural: an event has zero or many interested parties and the producer does not care who they are; a command has exactly one intended handler. A **producer** emits events without knowing who consumes them. A **consumer** subscribes and processes. A **broker** sits between, holding messages durably until consumers take them. The property that matters is **temporal decoupling**. In a synchronous call, producer and consumer must both be available at the same instant. With a broker, the producer publishes to a durable store; if every consumer is down, messages accumulate and are processed when consumers return. That buffering is what turns a cascading outage into a delay. ##### Queues, pub/sub, and streams Three distinct delivery models, frequently conflated. **Queue (work distribution).** Many consumers, but **each message goes to exactly one** of them. Messages are typically removed once acknowledged. This is a work-sharing model: five workers on one queue process five times as fast. Use for task distribution — send this email, generate this PDF, sync this record. **Pub/sub (broadcast).** Each message goes to **every** subscriber. Publishing `order.paid` delivers a copy to invoicing, email, analytics and warehouse independently. Classic pub/sub is fire-and-forget: a subscriber that is offline misses the message entirely. Use for event notification where multiple systems care about the same fact. **Stream (durable log).** Messages are appended to an ordered, replayable log and **retained** after consumption, for hours or days or forever. Consumers track their own **offset**. This combines pub/sub's fan-out with something neither queues nor pub/sub provide: **replay**. A new consumer can start from the beginning of history; a buggy consumer can be fixed and rewound. Use for event sourcing, analytics pipelines, and anywhere you might need to reprocess. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Q["Queue — one consumer per message"] P1[Producer] --> QQ[[queue]] QQ --> C1[Worker 1] QQ --> C2[Worker 2] end subgraph PS["Pub/Sub — every subscriber gets a copy"] P2[Producer] --> T{{topic}} T --> S1[Invoicing] T --> S2[Email] T --> S3[Analytics] end subgraph ST["Stream — durable, replayable log"] P3[Producer] --> L[(log: 0 1 2 3 4 5)] L --> G1[Group A
offset 5] L --> G2[Group B
offset 2 — replaying] end ``` ##### Redis, RabbitMQ, and Kafka | | Redis (Streams / Lists) | RabbitMQ | Kafka | |---|---|---|---| | **Model** | Queue + streams | Queue + pub/sub (exchanges) | Distributed log | | **Throughput** | Very high (in-memory) | High (~tens of k/s) | Extremely high (millions/s) | | **Latency** | Sub-millisecond | Low ms | Low ms | | **Durability** | Optional (AOF/RDB) — weakest | Strong, persistent queues | Strongest — replicated log on disk | | **Retention after read** | Configurable (streams) | No | Yes — days or forever | | **Replay** | Limited | No | First-class | | **Routing** | Basic | Excellent — topic/fanout/direct/headers | Partition key only | | **Ops burden** | Lowest | Moderate | Highest | **Redis** is the pragmatic default for automation workloads. You very likely run it already (n8n queue mode, Celery, caching), it is trivial to operate, and Redis Streams with consumer groups give you most of what you need. Its weakness is durability: an unconfigured Redis can lose recent messages on crash. **RabbitMQ** wins on **routing sophistication**. Topic exchanges let consumers subscribe to patterns like `order.*.india` or `*.failed`, with per-queue bindings, priorities, TTLs and native dead-letter exchanges. Choose it when message routing logic is genuinely complex. **Kafka** wins on **scale and replay**. Kreps et al.'s original 2011 paper framed it as a log for high-volume activity data, and that framing still explains when to choose it: enormous throughput, multiple independent consumer groups reading the same stream, and the ability to reprocess history. The cost is operational — brokers, partitions, ZooKeeper or KRaft, and a genuine learning curve. Do not run Kafka for 10,000 events a day. The honest recommendation for most automation work: **start with Redis, move to RabbitMQ if routing gets complicated, adopt Kafka when you need replay or your volume is genuinely large.** ##### Delivery guarantees Three levels, and only two are real. **At-most-once** — the message is delivered zero or one times. Fast, no retries, and messages are lost on failure. Acceptable only for disposable telemetry. **At-least-once** — the message is delivered one or more times. The broker redelivers if it does not receive an acknowledgment. **This is what essentially every production system uses**, and it means duplicates are guaranteed to occur eventually. **Exactly-once** — every message processed precisely once. In a distributed system with independent failures, true end-to-end exactly-once is not achievable in general. What systems label "exactly-once" is either broker-internal (Kafka's transactional producer, which covers writes back to Kafka) or, more usefully, **at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers**. That last phrase is the assignment's key point, and the reasoning is worth stating precisely. The failure that forces duplicates is unavoidable: a consumer processes a message successfully, then crashes *before* its acknowledgment reaches the broker. The broker cannot distinguish this from a consumer that died before processing. It must redeliver — anything else would lose messages. Therefore **the consumer must tolerate seeing the same message twice**, and that is a consumer-side obligation no broker can discharge for you. ```python import json, redis r = redis.Redis(host="localhost", decode_responses=True) STREAM, GROUP, DLQ = "orders", "processors", "orders:dlq" def consume(consumer_name: str) -> None: try: r.xgroup_create(STREAM, GROUP, id="0", mkstream=True) except redis.ResponseError: pass # group already exists while True: # '>' = only messages never delivered to this group resp = r.xreadgroup(GROUP, consumer_name, {STREAM: ">"}, count=10, block=5000) if not resp: reclaim_stale(consumer_name) # pick up crashed workers' messages continue for _stream, messages in resp: for msg_id, fields in messages: event = json.loads(fields["payload"]) try: # IDEMPOTENCY: SETNX returns False if the key already exists first_time = r.set(f"seen:{event['id']}", "1", nx=True, ex=86400) if first_time: handle(event) # real side effects here r.xack(STREAM, GROUP, msg_id) # ack only after success except TransientError: pass # no ack -> redelivered later except PermanentError as exc: r.xadd(DLQ, {"payload": fields["payload"], "error": str(exc)}) r.xack(STREAM, GROUP, msg_id) # ack: don't retry forever def reclaim_stale(consumer_name: str, idle_ms: int = 60_000) -> None: """Claim messages pending on dead consumers for more than idle_ms.""" r.xautoclaim(STREAM, GROUP, consumer_name, min_idle_time=idle_ms, start_id="0-0") ``` Three details carry the design. **Acknowledge only after successful processing** — acking first converts at-least-once into at-most-once. **`SET NX` is the idempotency gate**, atomic and race-free. And **`XAUTOCLAIM` handles crashed consumers**: messages pending too long on a dead worker are reassigned rather than stranded. ##### Dead-letter queues A **DLQ** is where messages go after exhausting retries. Without one you face two bad options: retry forever (blocking the queue and burning resources on a message that will never succeed) or drop silently (losing data). Design requirements: retain the **original payload plus the failure reason and attempt count**; **alert on DLQ depth**, because a growing DLQ is a signal that something systemic broke; and build a **replay path** so fixed messages can be re-injected. RabbitMQ has native dead-letter exchanges; with Redis or Kafka you implement it as a separate stream or topic. A subtlety worth knowing: distinguish **poison messages** (this one payload is malformed — DLQ it immediately) from **systemic failures** (the downstream API is down — retrying is correct). DLQ-ing everything during an outage turns a 20-minute blip into thousands of manual replays. ##### Backpressure, ordering, and consumer groups **Backpressure** is what happens when producers outpace consumers. Unmanaged, the queue grows until memory or disk is exhausted. Handle it by monitoring **queue depth and consumer lag** (the primary health metric for any broker), auto-scaling consumers on depth, bounding queue size with an explicit overflow policy, and rate-limiting producers where you control them. The queue itself is your shock absorber — but it has a capacity, and you need to know what happens when it fills. **Ordering** is guaranteed only within a partition or a single queue consumed serially. The moment you add a second consumer for throughput, global ordering is gone. The standard resolution is **partition by key**: route all events for `order_id=1042` to the same partition, so they are handled in sequence, while different orders process in parallel. Kafka does this natively via the message key. Failing that, make handlers order-independent — the version-guard technique from webhook work applies identically. **Consumer groups** are the mechanism that makes this work. Multiple consumers in one group share the partitions of a topic, each message going to exactly one group member. Different groups each get a full copy. So one Kafka topic can simultaneously feed a scaled-out invoicing group (work sharing) and an independent analytics group (fan-out) — queue and pub/sub semantics from one primitive. ##### Common pitfalls - **Acknowledging before processing**, silently downgrading to at-most-once. - **Non-idempotent consumers** under at-least-once delivery. - **No DLQ**, causing infinite retry loops or silent loss. - **Assuming global ordering** with parallel consumers. - **Ignoring consumer lag** until the disk fills. - **Using Kafka for small volumes** — operational cost with no benefit. - **Unbounded retries** on poison messages, blocking the queue head. - **Fat events** carrying whole documents; prefer an ID plus a fetch, or accept the payload size deliberately. - **No schema discipline** — an unversioned event shape breaks every consumer at once. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: stand up **Redis or RabbitMQ locally**, write a producer publishing events and a consumer processing them **idempotently**, then demonstrate **buffering** — stop the consumer, publish twenty events, restart it, and watch all twenty process. That buffering demo is the entire value proposition of a broker made visible in thirty seconds. The mini project is the full pipeline: a **webhook receiver publishing to a broker**, **multiple consumers in a consumer group** processing in parallel, **failures to a DLQ**, and **idempotent processing** — then prove it handles a burst without loss. Fire 1,000 events with a load tool, kill one consumer mid-run, and verify the final processed count is exactly 1,000 with zero duplicates. That test exercises consumer groups, redelivery, reclaim and idempotency all at once. For the assignment, compare **queues, pub/sub and streams**, then **Redis, RabbitMQ and Kafka** with a use case each, and explain **why at-least-once makes consumer idempotency mandatory**. For the last part, use the crash-after-processing-before-ack scenario — it is the concrete reason the obligation cannot be pushed onto the broker. ##### Key takeaways - Events are immutable facts, and a broker between producers and consumers provides temporal decoupling — the property that stops one slow service taking down a whole chain. - Queues distribute work one-message-one-consumer; pub/sub broadcasts to all subscribers; streams add retention and replay via consumer-managed offsets. - Redis is the pragmatic default for automation, RabbitMQ wins on routing sophistication, Kafka on throughput and replay — and is overkill below serious volume. - Production systems are at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent: ack only after success, and gate side effects on an atomic seen-check. - Give every pipeline a DLQ with payload, error and attempt count; monitor consumer lag as your primary health metric; and partition by key when ordering matters.
practical_task_reference: Stand up Redis (or RabbitMQ) locally and build a producer that publishes events and a consumer that processes them idempotently, demonstrating buffering when the consumer is temporarily stopped and then resumes.
mini_project_reference: Build an event-driven pipeline: a webhook receiver publishes events to a broker, multiple worker consumers process them in parallel (consumer group), failures go to a dead-letter queue, and processing is idempotent - then demonstrate it handling a burst of events without loss.
assignment_reference: Compare queues, pub/sub, and streams and compare Redis, RabbitMQ, and Kafka, giving a use case for each, and explain why at-least-once delivery makes consumer idempotency mandatory.
